title: 3D Home Building
desc: Understand how large-scale 3D printing of walls and homes works, its safety, codes, costs and where it suits.
outcomes: Explain how a construction printer builds walls.
Write a feasibility note for a small building.
task: Write a feasibility note for a small printed building with design, quantities, time, cost, code checks and risks.
condition: A computer, public information, a spreadsheet, two peers and a mentor builder. No printer operation is done.
standard: Quantities and time are calculated; code and permit checks are listed; risks and controls are stated; cost compared with conventional building; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Builders, architects in training, housing groups, students.
evidence: quantity sheet, cost comparison, risk list, note
modules: How a construction printer works
Understand
A construction 3D printer builds walls by laying a cement-like mix in layers, following a digital path.
A gantry or robotic arm moves a nozzle over the site, or parts are printed off site and lifted into place.
Walls are printed in layers of about 15 to 40 mm; foundations, doors, windows, roof and services are added by trades.
A design file controls the path; changing the file changes the building.
Printing is fast for walls, but the whole building still needs foundations, roof and finishes.
A printer lays a 40 mm bead in a double-wall pattern with hollow cavities. The cavities are later filled with reinforcement and insulation. A precast printed planter is made off site in two hours.
Draw the process from design file to finished wall and compare on-site and off-site printing.
Steps are in order and both options are compared.
Printable materials and curing
Understand
The mix decides success.
Cement-based mixes with additives, earth mixes and recycled aggregates.
The mix must flow through the nozzle, hold its shape under the next layer and gain strength.
Hot, dry or windy weather dries layers too fast; cold slows curing.
Test every batch for flow and strength.
On a hot day a retarder is added so layers bond before drying. A 1 m test wall is printed and cut open; poor bonding is found at low temperature.
Compare two mixes in a table and describe a test wall plan.
Properties and limits are listed.
Design, engineering and building codes
Apply
Printed buildings follow the same safety rules as other buildings.
Structural design by a qualified engineer, including reinforcement, openings and loads such as wind and earthquake.
Fire, energy, accessibility and ventilation codes.
Foundations and services as usual.
Permits and inspections before, during and after printing.
Steel bars are placed in wall cavities before they are filled, and an engineer signs the design. Vertical rebar is added every 600 mm for an earthquake zone.
List code checks and loads for a small building in your place.
Sources are listed and loads are named.
Quantities, time and cost drivers
Analyse
Count the bead and the hours.
Wall length x height / layer height = layers.
Volume x density = material mass; add 10 per cent for waste.
Print speed gives hours; add set-up and clean-up time.
Include transport of the machine and mix.
60 m of wall at 3 m high with 20 mm layers needs 150 layers; at 4 minutes a layer that is 10 hours plus 1 hour set-up.
Calculate quantities and time for a small room.
Maths is correct with waste and set-up included.
Site safety
Evaluate
People and machines share the site.
Exclusion zones, emergency stop and lifting plans.
Dust and silica protection when cutting or mixing.
Weather plan and training.
A trained operator and a spotter at all times.
A fence marks the print zone and two workers are assigned: operator and spotter.
Write a site safety plan with roles.
Plan is approved by a mentor.
Cost and comparison with conventional building
Evaluate
See where it pays.
Labour saved versus machine, material and transport cost.
Speed and waste reduction.
Compare per square metre of wall and of the whole building.
Doors, roof and finishes cost the same either way.
Printed walls cost 12 per cent less, but doors and roofing cost the same, so the whole building saves about 4 per cent. Transport of the machine adds 8 per cent to the first project.
Build a comparison table for one small building.
Currency shown and assumptions listed.
Quality control and records
Apply
Test and record.
Sample cubes for strength and a slump or flow test for every batch.
Check layer bonding and tolerances.
Record mix temperature, weather and batch numbers.
Fix defects before covering.
A cube fails the strength test and the batch is rejected; the log shows mix water was too high.
Write a quality control plan with tests and records.
Tests are named and records defined.
Feasibility note
Create
Bring it all together.
Fit: housing, shelters, sheds and small buildings.
Risks, permits and next steps.
List ten questions for a mentor builder.
Recommend go, pilot or stop.
The note recommends a small pilot hut before a house, and a builder advises testing in your climate first.
Write and present the note.
Reader can decide from the note.
quiz: How is a wall built?
In layers by a gantry or arm. (Covered in module 1: How a construction printer works. To pass that module: Steps are in order and both options are compared.)
What controls the path?
A design file. (Covered in module 2: Printable materials and curing. To pass that module: Properties and limits are listed.)
Who designs structure?
An engineer. (Covered in module 3: Design, engineering and building codes. To pass that module: Sources are listed and loads are named.)
Layers formula?
Height / layer height. (Covered in module 4: Quantities, time and cost drivers. To pass that module: Maths is correct with waste and set-up included.)
Silica danger?
Dust harms lungs. (Covered in module 5: Site safety. To pass that module: Plan is approved by a mentor.)
Why cube tests?
Check strength. (Covered in module 6: Cost and comparison with conventional building. To pass that module: Currency shown and assumptions listed.)
What stays manual?
Roof and services. (Covered in module 7: Quality control and records. To pass that module: Tests are named and records defined.)
Weather effect?
Curing changes. (Covered in module 8: Feasibility note. To pass that module: Reader can decide from the note.)
Cost comparison unit?
Per m2. (Covered in module 8: Feasibility note. To pass that module: Reader can decide from the note.)
Why pilot?
Learn small. (Covered in module 8: Feasibility note. To pass that module: Reader can decide from the note.)
